messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Photographer
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 18, Minh had already built a life around looking through a lens. He was a young Southeast Asian American photographer who spent long hours moving through city streets, school gyms, parking lots, and neighborhood events with a camera hanging against his chest, catching moments other people missed. Before treatment, he described the combat experience as something that did not feel finished or distant, but as if it remained waiting just behind whatever he was doing. When he spoke about it, the memory did not come in the softened way he remembered ordinary parts of childhood or recent days. It arrived with a sharpness that made him stop mid-sentence, as though he were seeing it rather than recalling it.

In the combat incident he described, the defining moment was not only that he was under attack, but that other people were with him and he believed he had a responsibility to keep them alive. In his account, there was a sudden eruption of noise and confusion, the kind of scene where the body reacts before the mind can catch up. He remembered explosive sound, shouted warnings, movement, and the split-second realization that others were exposed and he could not get to everyone in time. What stayed with him most was the conviction that he had failed at the exact moment protection mattered. He did not recount the event like a completed story with a beginning and end; he returned to the instant of danger and his own furious certainty that he should have done more.

In the months afterward, ordinary sounds became charged in ways he could not predict. A dropped metal stand during a photo shoot, a car backfiring in the street, someone slamming a door in the studio building could make his whole body jolt before he knew what had happened. He hated how visible this was. While assistants or clients laughed off a noise, Minh was already tense, scanning, and ashamed of reacting so fast. Even in settings he knew were safe, he could not settle. He would sit editing photos late at night in his room, shoulders locked, listening for sounds in the hallway or outside the window, telling himself there was no threat and finding that his body refused to believe him.

Because his work kept him out in the world, he encountered reminders constantly and without warning. The crack of celebratory fireworks over a community event, the rapid percussion of equipment cases being unloaded, the sight of young men moving in formation for a school sports media day—small details in his surroundings could pull the combat scene over the present moment with brutal speed. When that happened, the memory felt more real than what was in front of him. He described it as if the past surged forward and the current scene lost substance. With that return came intense rage: rage at what had happened, at the people involved, at himself for not having prevented the losses he believed were his to prevent. He was often more frightened by the force of that anger than by the memory itself.

Outside of work, he had begun taking risks that worried the people around him. He moved through traffic on his motorcycle too fast, climbed unstable structures to get dramatic shots, and entered unfamiliar areas alone at odd hours without much concern for his safety. He did not present these choices as thrill-seeking. They came across more as a loosening of self-protection, as if danger no longer registered in the usual way or no longer mattered enough to avoid. At the same time, he trusted almost no one. If someone offered help on a shoot or tried to get close to him personally, Minh assumed there would be a cost, a betrayal, or a moment when they would prove unreliable. Being single felt less like circumstance than confirmation of what he had come to believe: that he no longer belonged anywhere, not with civilians who had no reference for what he carried, and not fully with others from the combat setting either, because in his mind he had failed the most basic obligation there.

That belief had begun to affect his work. Photography had once given him a place among people, but lately he kept interactions transactional and brief. He turned down collaborative jobs, left events early after being thrown by unexpected noise, and alienated a repeat client after snapping when equipment clattered to the floor behind him. What finally brought him to seek help was not one dramatic collapse but the accumulation of these moments: the jumpiness he could not hide, the anger that came roaring up with the memory, the sense that he was drifting further from everyone who tried to know him. He came in convinced that people could not be trusted and unsure whether therapy would be any different, but he also seemed tired of living as though every ordinary sound might open the whole scene again. What frightened him most was the possibility that this was permanent—that he would remain stranded between the vividness of that moment and a present life in which he no longer felt he belonged.
